Karma is irrelevant, right?

News aggregator-type sites (such as voat, reddit, digg, etc) allow people to bring together interesting content, based on the feedback of the other users of the site.

I understand why the links have karma - they require some kind of quanitative measure to allow the good stuff to rise above the mediocre. But why is the karma of a submitted link associated with the user who submitted it? Shouldn't the content stand on it's own? If I post something, should it really matter if I have 0 or 1,000,000 karma behind me? Would you stop posting if you didn't receive imaginary internet points?

The way I see it, karma is only destructive -

  • if karma is used for positioning articles, "super-users" with lots of karma can have a ridiculously huge impact on the site's content (anyone remember mrbabyman on digg?)

  • it encourages users to create dummy accounts to upvoat themselves (e.g. unidan)

  • it fuels negative associations between people (e.g. going through someone's posting history and downvoating everything there)

  • it encourages re-posts

What am I missing? What is the purpose of user-karma? Can someone explain how it is beneficial?

I think it's important to make the distinction between karma being an influence and it being a measure of how much other people like what you post.

While I do think there is something to be said when it comes to post vs. comment points, I think the admins here have taken steps to mitigate a lot of the points you raise.

It is true that by having user karma, karma-hungry manipulators like unidan could be inclined to do what they do. But, I'm not sure removing the karma counter from user profiles would prevent this type of behavior because karma would still be displayed on comments. Sure, it's not globally accounted for, but, in the same way that popular subreddits on Reddit are populated with many low-effort karma-grabbing comments, the same could be repeated here and gain many upvotes. Inevitably, we would see power users become well known or even famous across many subs by repeating their popular opinions. Other users will see this and some would perpetuate the behavior, bringing the general comment quality into a nose dive.

So, I guess my point here is that, if the existence of accumulated user karma should be argued against, the way the whole numerically-displayed karma system works should also be argued against by association, if the main counter point is "preventing users from manipulating the system to gain karma", or similar.
